passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Σίμων Οὐκοῦν [εἰ] ὁ. θεὸς μόνων τῶν καλῶν αἴτιός ἐστιν, τοῦ λοιποῦ τί ἐστιν νοεῖν ἢ ὅτι τὸ πονηρὸν ἑτέρα τις ἐγέννησεν ἀρχὴ ἢ ἄρ’ ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὔτε ἑτέρα τις δύναμις ἐγέννησεν τὸν πονηρὸν οὔτε ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν τὸ κακόν, ὡς ἐπὶ τέλει δείξω· νῦν γὰρ ἀποδεῖξαί μοι πρόκειται (ὡς ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ὑπεσχόμην) ὅτι κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ὁ θεὸς ἄμεμπτός ἐστιν. δεδώκαμεν οὖν ὅτι ὁ θεὸς τῶν ἀνθρώποις προσόντων τὰ κρείττονα ἀσυγκρίτως ἔχει. διὸ καὶ ἐνδέχεται αὐτὸν προβολέα γενέσθαι τῶν τεσσάρων οὐσιῶν, θερμοῦ [λέγω] καὶ ψυχροῦ, ὑγροῦ τε καὶ ξηροῦ. [ταῦτ]α μὲν ὡς πρῶτα ἁπλᾶ καὶ ἀμιγῆ [ὄντ]α πρὸς οὐδέτερον ἔχει τὴν ὄρε[ξιν], προβληθέντα δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ [κ]αὶ ἔξω κραθέντα γενέσθαι ζῷον, προ[αί]ρεσιν ἔχον ὀλοθρεῦσαι κακούς. καὶ οὕτως ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντων γεγεννημένων, ὁ πονηρὸς οὔτε ἄλλοθέν ἐστιν οὔτε ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πάντα πεποιηκότος θεοῦ τὴν κακίαν εἴληφεν, παρ’ ᾧ ὑπάρχειν ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, ὅτι αἱ μὲν οὐσίαι οὐδέτεραι οὖσαι, πεφιλοκρινημέναι ἐξ αὐτοῦ προβέβληνται, καὶ ἔξω αὐταῖς κραθείσαις ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτοῦ τέχνης βουλήσει συμβέβηκεν ἡ πρὸς τὸν τῶν κακῶν ὄλεθρον ἐπιθυμία — ἀγαθοὺς δὲ ἡ συμβεβηκυῖα κακία ὀλοθρεῦσαι οὐ δύναται, οὐδ’ εἰ βουληθείη· νόμῳ γὰρ κατὰ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχει. ἀγνοῶν οὖν τὸν ἑκάστου τρόπον τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν λαμβάνει [ἐμ]πειρίαν καὶ διελέγξας τιμωρεῖ. κ[αὶ ὁ Σ[ί]μων ἔφη Δυνατὸς οὖν ὑπάρχων ὁ [θεὸς] κιρνᾶν τὰ στοιχεῖα, καὶ ποιεῖν κράσει[ς] πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις, διὰ τί μὴ ἀγαθῶν προαιρετι[κὴν] ἐποίει τὴν ἑκάστου κρᾶσιν;

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ταῦτα μὲν ὀρθῶς ἔφης· πλὴν ἐν τῷ νῦν κόσμῳ οὐ δοκεῖ σοι παντὸς πάθους δεκτικὸς εἶναι ὁ ἄνθρωπος; λέγω δὲ ἐπιθυμίας, ὀργῆς, λύπης καὶ τῶν τοιούτων. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Καὶ ταῦτα τῶν·συμβαινόντων ἐστίν, οὐ τῶν ἀεὶ ὄντων· χρησίμως δὲ τῇ ψυχῇ συμβαίνοντα νῦν εὑρεθήσεται. ἥ τε γὰρ ἐπιθυμία ἐκ τοῦ πάντα καλῶς δημιουργήσαντος συμβαίνειν τῷ ζῴῳ γεγένηται, ἵνα ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀγόμενον πρὸς κοινωνίαν τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα πληθύνῃ, ἀφ’ ἧς πλῆθος ἐκλογῆς κρειττόνων γίνεται πρὸς αἰώνιον ζωὴν ἐπιτήδειον. πλὴν ἄνευ ἐπιθυμίας τὴν πρὸς γυναῖκα κοινωνίαν οὐδεὶς ἂν ἀνεδέξατο, νῦν δὲ προφάσει ἡδονῆς ὡς ἑαυτῷ χαριζόμενος ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα ποιεῖ. πλὴν ἐάν τις τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ χρῆται πρὸς νόμιμον γάμον, οὐκ ἀσεβεῖ· πρὸς μοιχείαν δὲ ὁρμῶν δυσσεβεῖ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τιμωρεῖται, ὅτι τῷ καλῶς τεθέντι ἐχρήσατο κακῶς. ἔτι τε ὁμοίως ἡ ὀργὴ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξάπτεσθαι φύσιν ἔχειν εἴληφε παρὰ θεοῦ, ἵνα πρὸς ἄμυναν ἁμαρτημάτων ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἑλκώμεθα. πλὴν ἀμέτρῳ αὐτῇ τις χρησάμενος ἀδικεῖ, κατ’ ἀξίαν δὲ χρώμενος τὸ δίκαιον ἐκτελεῖ. ἀλλὰ καὶ λύπης ἐσμὲν δεκτικοί, ἵνα τὸ συμπαθητικὸν ἔχωμεν ἐπί τε θανάτῳ, οἰκείων, γυναικὸς ἢ τέκνων ἢ ἀδελ-. φῶν ἢ γονέων ἢ φίλων ἢ ἄλλων τινῶν· ἐπείπερ εἰ τὸ συμπάσχειν οὐκ εἴχομεν, ἀπάνθρωποι ἂν ἦμεν. ὁμῶς καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα οἰκείως εὑρεθήσεται ἔχοντα, ἐάν γε διὸ γέγονε νοηθῇ.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἄωροι τελευτῶσι καὶ περιοδικαὶ νόσοι γίνονται, ἔτι μὴν καὶ δαίμονες καὶ μανίαι καὶ πάθη παντοδαπά, κολάζειν μεγάλως δυνάμενα, ὑπάρχει; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ὅτι. οἱ ἄνθρωποι τὰ πάντα αὐτῶν τῇ ἡδονῇ χαριζόμενοι ἀπαρατηρήτως κοινωνοῦσι καὶ οὕτως ἡ τῶν σπερμάτων καταβολὴ ἀκαίρως ἐπιδοθεῖσα φυσικῶς τὰ μυρία ἐκφύει κακά. ἐχρῆν δὲ αὐτοὺς λογίζεσθαι ὅτι ὡς τοῦ φυτεῦσαι καὶ σπεῖραι καιρὸς ἐπιτήδειος ὥρισται, οὕτω καὶ τοῦ κοινωνῆσαι ἐπιτηρήσιμοι ἡμέραι προσῳκείωνται. ἔνθεν γοῦν τις ἐκ τῆς Μωϋσέως παραδόσεως μεμαθηκώς, αἰτιώμενος τὸν λαὸν ἐπὶ ἁμαρτίαις, υἱοὺς νεομηνιῶν τῶν κατὰ σελήνην καὶ σαββάτων ἀπεκάλει. ἀλλὰ καὶ κατ’ ἀρχὰς τοῦ κόσμου οἱ ἄνθρωποι πολυετεῖς τε ἦσαν καὶ ἄνοσοι· ὁπότε δὲ ἀμελήσαντες τὴν παρατήρησιν ἀπέλιπον, ἔκτοτε κατὰ διαδοχὴν υἱοὶ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ ..... μὴ δεῖν κοινωνοῦντες ὑπὸ μυρία πάθη τὰ ἑαυτῶν τιθέασι τέκνα. ὅθεν καὶ ..... αλος ἡμῶν περὶ τοῦ ἐκ γενετῆς πηροῦ καὶ ἀναβλέψαντος παρ’ αὐτοῦ’ ἔξετα .............. εν οὗτος ἢ οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη, ἀπεκρίνατο „οὔτε οὗτός τι ἥμαρτεν οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἵνα δι’ αὐτοῦ φανερωθῇ ἡ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ“ τῆς ἀγνοίας ἰωμένη τὰ ἁμαρτήματα. καὶ ἀληθῶς ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ τὰ τοιαῦτα γίνεται ἤτοι τῷ μὴ εἰδέναι πότε δεῖ κοινωνεῖν τῇ γαμετῇ, εἰ καθαρὰ ἐξ ἀφέδρου τυγχάνει. πλὴν ἃ προείρηκας πάθη ἐξ ἀγνοίας ἐστίν, οὐ μέντοι ἐκ πονηροῦ εἰργασμένα. προσέτι δὲ δὸς τὸν μὴ ἁμαρτάνοντα καὶ λαβὲ τὸν μὴ πάσχοντα, καὶ πρὸς τὸ μὴ πάσχειν καὶ ἄλλους αὐτὸν θεραπεῦσαι δυνάμενος εὕρῃς. αὐτίκα γοῦν Μωϋσῆς διὰ εὐσέβειαν ἀπαθὴς τὸν πάντα τῆς ζωῆς διετέλεσε χρόνον καὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους δι’ ἁμαρτίας πάσχοντας εὐχαῖς ἰᾶτο.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἔστω μὲν ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχειν· οὐ δοκεῖ σοι ἀδικωτάτη ἡ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀνωμαλία; ὃς μὲν γὰρ πένεται, ὃς δὲ πλουτεῖ — καὶ ὃς μὲν νοσεῖ καὶ ..... ὑγιαίνει — καὶ ὅμως τοιαῦτά τινα μυρία ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐ συνορᾷς, ὦ Σίμων, ὅτι πάλιν ἐκτὸς τοῦ σκοποῦ τοὺς λόγους πέμπεις; περὶ πονηροῦ γὰρ ἡμῶν διαλεγομένων, σὺ ἐκτροπὴν ποιήσας περὶ τῶν δοκούντων ἀτοπημάτων τὸν λόγον εἰσηγήσω· πλὴν καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ ἐρῶ. ὁ κόσμος ὄργανόν ἐστι τεχνικῶς γεγονός, ἵνα τῷ ἐσομένῳ ἄρρενι αἰωνίως ἡ θήλεια τίκτῃ δικαίους αἰωνίους υἱούς. οὐκ ἐδύναντο δὲ εὐσεβεῖς ἐνταῦθα ἀποτελεσθῆναι, εἰ μὴ ἦσαν οἱ ἐνδεεῖς οἷς ἐπικουρήσουσιν — ὁμοίως τε καὶ διὰ τοῦτό εἰσι καὶ νοσοῦντες, ὧν προνοήσουσι — καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς τοῦτον περιέχει τὸν λόγον. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Οὐκοῦν ἠτύχηται τοῖς ταπεινοῖς· πρὸς γὰρ τὸ ἀποτελεσθῆναι δικαίους αὐτοὶ κακουχοῦνται. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἰ ἦν αἰώνιος ταπείνωσις αὐτῶν, ἀτυχία ἂν ἡ μεγίστη· ἀλλὰ πρὸς τῷ κλήρῳ τὰ ταπεινώματα καὶ ὑψώματα ἀνθρώποις γίνεται· ᾧ δ’ ἂν μὴ ἀρέσκῃ ὁ κλῆρος, ἔνεστιν ἐκκλήτῳ χρησάμενον καὶ νομίμως διαδικασάμενον αὐτὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ὑπαλλάξαι βίον. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Τίς οὗτος ὁ κλῆρος καὶ ἔκκλητος; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Τοῦτο ἑτέρου λόγου ἐξήγησίς ἐστι· πλὴν ἐὰν ἐπιτρέψῃς, δεῖξαί σοι δυνάμεθα πῶς ἀναγεννηθεὶς καὶ τὴν γένεσιν ὑπαλλάξας καὶ νομίμως βιώσας αἰωνίου τεύξῃ σωτηρίας.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ταῦτα ἀκούσας ἔφη Μήτι νομίσῃς ὡς ἐπειδὴ εἰς ἕκαστον κεφάλαιον ζητῶν συνετιθέμην, ὡς πληροφορούμενος ἐφ’ ἕτερον ἠρχόμην κεφάλαιον, ἀλ.....νοίας σοι τοῦ πείθεσθαι παρεῖχον, ἵνα ἐπ’ ἄλλο ἔλθῃς κεφάλαιον, ὅπως πάσας ......... νοίας σου μαθών, μὴ στοχαζόμενος καταγινώσκω σου. ἀλλὰ πεπληροφορημε ............ νῦν δὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν μοι συγχώρησον καὶ ἐλθὼν δείξω σε μηδὲν εἰδότα. ταῦτα τοῦ Σίμωνος εἰπόντος καὶ ἐξιέναι μέλλοντος ὁ ἐμὸς ἔφη πατὴρ Βραχέα μου, Σίμων, ἐπακούσας, ὥς σοι φίλον ἐστί, πορεύου. μέμνημαι ὡς τὴν ἀρχὴν πρὸ τῆς ζητήσεως ὡς μήπω πεῖράν μου λαβὼν προλήψεις μου κατέφερες. καὶ νῦν δὲ ἐπαλλήλως ἀκούσας τῆς ζητήσεως καὶ Πέτρον ἐν ὑπεροχῇ γνοὺς καὶ αὐτῷ τὸ ἀληθεύειν νῦν δούς, καὶ τί σοι φαίνομαι; ὀρθῶς κρίνειν εἰδὼς ἢ οὔ; εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὀρθῶς κρίναντά με φαίης, μὴ συνθῇ δέ: σὺ φαίνῃ προειλημμένος, ὁ καὶ μετὰ ὁμολογίαν . ἦτταν συνθέσθαι μὴ θέλων. εἰ δ’ ἄρα μὴ ὀρθῶς τὸν Πέτρον ἐν ὑπεροχῇ τῆς ζητήσεως ἀπεφαινόμην: σὺ ἡμᾶς πεῖσον πῶς οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἐκρίναμεν — ἢ τοῦ ζητεῖν αὐτῷ ἐπὶ πάντων μὴ παύσῃ, ἐπεὶ ἔσται σοι (ἑκάστοτε ἠττωμένῳ καὶ συντιθεμένῳ, εἰ δὲ τὸ αἰδεῖσθαι ἔχεις, ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἀκροατῶν ἀντὶ μεγίστης τιμωρίας καταγινωσκομένῳ καὶ ἀσχημονοῦντι) ὑπὸ συνειδήσεως τὴν σεαυτοῦ ἀλγεῖν ψυχήν· τὸ γὰρ νενικῆσθαί σε ἔργῳ εἴδομεν, τὸν δὲ ἐπαγγελλόμενόν σου λόγον ἠκούσαμεν. πέρας γοῦν οὐκ οἶμαί σε ἐπὶ τὴν ζήτησιν ἐλθεῖν, ὡς ὑπέσχου, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ δοκεῖν μὴ αἰδεῖσθαι ἐξιὼν ἐπανελθεῖν ὑπέσχησαι.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model

passages.text: Simon said, “Then, if God is responsible only for good things, what remains to be understood except that some other principle produced evil, or perhaps it is ungenerated?” Peter said, “Neither did some other power produce the evil one, nor is evil ungenerated, as I will show at the end. For now my task is to demonstrate, as I promised at the beginning, that God is blameless in every way. We have granted, then, that God possesses the better things that belong to human beings incomparably. Therefore it is also possible for him to be the one who sends forth the four substances—I mean the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry. These, being primary, simple, and unmixed, have an appetite for neither side. But, sent forth by God and mixed outside, they can become a living being with a choice to destroy evil people. Thus, though everything has been produced from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his wickedness from God himself, who made everything. Wickedness cannot exist with him, because the substances, being neutral, were separated out and sent forth from him. When, outside, they were mixed by his skill at his will, the desire for the destruction of evil people occurred. But the wickedness that occurred cannot destroy good people, even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. So, not knowing each person’s character, he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them.” Simon said, “Since God is capable of mixing the elements and making mixtures for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise, why did he not make each person’s constitution inclined to choose good things?”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun describes an emitter or producer by projection; “emanator” is a technical alternative. The main text retains sending-forth language, not a claim that the passage explicitly teaches creation from nothing.

The statement concerns superior qualities among those attributed to humans. “Possesses incomparably superior qualities” is a more idiomatic alternative, but the main text preserves the comparative and the separate adverb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have an appetite for neither side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two sides can be understood as good and evil in the argument; neither is inserted as a newly printed noun.

The unusual perfect participle conveys distinction or separation of the substances in this argument. “Carefully distinguished” is possible, but a claim of affectionate separation is not imposed merely from the compound’s form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν λαμβάνει [ἐμ]πειρίαν καὶ διελέγξας τιμωρεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hostile κατ’ αὐτῶν is retained. Contextually this can be rendered “he tests them and, after proving their wrongdoing, punishes them”; the main text does not add a specific trial method or identify the implicit object of exposure more narrowly than the people concerned.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both overlapping purpose/relative phrases are represented, not reduced to a single clause. The second feminine relative anticipates the plural choices.

It is not silently normalized, claimed as an OCR error, or used to invent any missing words. The other square brackets in this passage supply portions of words as printed, rather than dot-count gaps.

passages.text: Simon said, “You have said these things correctly. Yet in the present world, does it not seem to you that a human being is susceptible to every passion? I mean desire, anger, grief, and such things.” Peter said, “These too belong to the things that happen, not to the things that always exist. They will now be found to occur usefully for the soul. For desire has been made to occur in the living being by the one who made everything well, so that, led by it into intercourse, it may multiply humanity. From humanity a multitude of chosen better people arises, suitable for eternal life. But without desire no one would have undertaken intercourse with a woman; as it is, under the pretext of pleasure, as though gratifying himself, the human being does that one’s will. Yet if someone uses desire for lawful marriage, he does not act impiously. If he rushes toward adultery, he acts impiously and for this reason is punished, because he used badly what was established well. Likewise, anger has received from God the nature of being kindled within us, so that we may be drawn by it to resist sins. Yet someone who uses it without measure does wrong, while one who uses it as deserved accomplishes what is just. We are also susceptible to grief, so that we may have sympathy at the death of members of our household—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or anyone else. For if we did not have the capacity to share suffering, we would be inhuman. All the other things likewise will be found to be fitting, if the reason why they came into being is understood.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Occurrences are contrasted with things existing always; “accidents” in a technical philosophical sense is possible but misleading without explanation.

The immediate purpose of multiplying humanity supports the sexual sense of participation or sharing here. The text adds no sexual detail or named partners beyond the ensuing woman and lawful marriage.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a multitude of chosen better people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact genitives can alternatively mean “a multitude from which better people are selected.” The main text takes ἐκλογῆς as characterizing the resultant multitude by selection, retaining κρειττόνων as the selected better people; it does not uniquely settle how the selection is made.
ἄμυνα can mean defense against or requital of offenses. The main text takes the first, while “to punish offenses” is a material alternative in view of the ensuing measured use of anger.
The term can indicate proportional worth or due measure; the main text does not make every expression of anger just.

passages.text: Simon said, “Why, then, do people also die before their time, and why do recurring illnesses arise? Moreover, why are there demons, madness, and sufferings of every kind, capable of inflicting great punishment?” Peter said, “Because people devote everything of their own to pleasure, have intercourse without observing the proper times, and thus the depositing of seed, offered at the wrong time, naturally grows countless evils. They should have reasoned that, just as a suitable time for planting and sowing has been appointed, so days requiring observance have been assigned for intercourse. Hence someone who had learned from the tradition of Moses, reproaching the people for sins, called them sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths. At the beginning of the world people were also long-lived and free of illness. But when, through neglect, they abandoned the observance, from that time sons in succession, because of ignorance, ..... having intercourse when they should not, place their own children under countless sufferings. Hence also our [..... αλος], concerning the person disabled from birth who received sight from him, [ἔξετα .............. εν] this man or his parents, he was born blind, answered, ‘Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents, but so that through him the power of God might be revealed,’ healing the sins of ignorance. And indeed such things happen because of ignorance: that is, not knowing when one should have intercourse with one’s wife, whether she is clean from menstruation. Yet the sufferings you mentioned come from ignorance; they are not, however, brought about by the evil one. Moreover, give me someone who does not sin, and receive someone who does not suffer; and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well. Moses, for example, through reverence for God continued without suffering throughout his whole life, and by prayers healed the Egyptians who suffered because of sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: have intercourse without observing the proper times
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following planting analogy and days to observe specify the context of observance; “without precaution” is less specific. This is the ancient speaker’s explanation, not independent medical advice.
The adjective denotes periodic or cyclical occurrence, not a specific diagnosis.
The historical categories are retained, not collapsed into a modern psychiatric equivalence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: υἱοὺς νεομηνιῶν τῶν κατὰ σελήνην καὶ σαββάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source explicitly connects the days with the sons in its argument. No prophet’s name or external quotation is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε οὗτός τι ἥμαρτεν οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: This rendering follows the wording of this author’s quotation, without importing differently worded biblical translations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whether she is clean from menstruation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purity category is the speaker’s, not an added biological assertion. “Whether she has become clean after menstruation” is another contextual rendering.
The feminine participle can agree with δύναμις, power, in the quotation; its action is not assigned to a uniquely named person by the English.

source_issues.source_quote: υἱοὶ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ ..... μὴ δεῖν κοινωνοῦντες
source_issues.issue: The five-dot printed gap is retained exactly. The sentence stays visibly incomplete at the link between the sons, ignorance, and intercourse that should not take place; no missing connective or argument is restored.
The five-dot gap and surviving αλος are retained literally as [..... αλος]. The partial word is not completed to a title or person’s name.

source_issues.source_quote: ἔξετα .............. εν οὗτος ἢ οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη
source_issues.issue: The surviving ἔξετα and εν flank a fourteen-dot printed gap, all retained literally as [ἔξετα .............. εν]. The subsequent surviving “this man or his parents” and “he was born blind” are represented as incomplete syntax, not joined by a restored question about sin from an external biblical text. No lost words are recovered.

passages.text: Simon said, “Let these things be so. Does the inequality among people not seem most unjust to you? For one is poor and another rich; one is ill and ..... is healthy; and there are countless such things in human life.” Peter said, “Do you not see, Simon, that again you are sending your arguments beyond the aim? For while we are discussing the evil one, you have turned aside and introduced an argument about what seem to be anomalies. Yet I will speak to this too. The world is an instrument made with skill, so that the female may eternally bear righteous, eternal sons for the male who is to come. But reverent people could not be brought to completion here unless there were people in need whom they might assist. Likewise, this is also why there are sick people whom they might care for. And the following matters contain this same rationale.” Simon said, “Then the lowly have suffered misfortune: they themselves suffer hardship so that righteous people may be brought to completion.” Peter said, “If their lowliness were eternal, it would be the greatest misfortune. But people’s low conditions and high conditions occur in accordance with their allotted lot. Anyone whose lot does not please him can make use of an appeal and, pleading his case according to law, change his life through it.” Simon said, “What is this lot and appeal?” Peter said, “That is the explanation belonging to another discussion. But if you permit it, we can show you how, being born anew, changing your birth-destiny, and living according to law, you will obtain eternal salvation.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐσομένῳ ἄρρενι αἰωνίως ἡ θήλεια τίκτῃ δικαίους αἰωνίους υἱούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the female may eternally bear righteous, eternal sons for the male who is to come
lexical_decisions.rationale: The symbolic male and female are not identified as God, the world, the Messiah, or any specific persons not named in this clause. The main text attaches αἰωνίως to bearing, preserving continual or eternal generation; it can alternatively qualify the male’s future existence: “for the male who will exist eternally.” The sons’ explicit adjective αἰωνίους is retained separately.
κλῆρος denotes an allotted portion, not necessarily chance or an already specified astrological mechanism. Its precise explanation is deferred by Peter himself.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκκλήτῳ χρησάμενον καὶ νομίμως διαδικασάμενον αὐτὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ὑπαλλάξαι βίον
lexical_decisions.chosen: make use of an appeal and, pleading his case according to law, change his life through it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The legal appeal and adjudication imagery is preserved. ἔκκλητος can refer to an appeal or an appellate authority; accordingly ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ can mean “through it” or “by him,” the agent handling the appeal. The main text does not identify a particular tribunal or human judge.

γένεσις can mean birth or origin; with allotted conditions and rebirth here, birth-destiny keeps both associations visible. “Changing your birth” is the more literal alternative, while “changing your natal fate” is more specifically astrological.

source_issues.issue: The five-dot gap is preserved exactly between illness and being healthy. The subject for the latter verb is missing from the surviving sequence and is not filled by an invented “another.”

passages.text: When Simon heard these things, he said, “Do not suppose that, because in examining each topic I agreed, I was proceeding to another topic because I was fully convinced. I was providing you [ἀλ.....νοίας] of being persuaded, so that you would move to another topic, in order that, having learned all your [......... νοίας], I might condemn you without guessing. But [πεπληροφορημε ............]. Now allow me three days, and I will come and show that you know nothing.” After Simon said this and was about to leave, my father said, “Simon, hear a few words from me, and then go as you please. I remember that at the beginning, before the inquiry, having not yet tested me, you leveled preconceived judgments against me. But now, after hearing the discussion continuously, recognizing Peter’s superiority, and now granting him truthfulness, what do I seem to you? Someone who knows how to judge rightly, or not? For if you say that I judged rightly but do not agree, you appear prejudiced, unwilling even after acknowledgment to agree to defeat. But if I did not rightly declare Peter superior in the inquiry, persuade us how we judged incorrectly—or do not stop debating with him before everyone. For, each time being defeated and agreeing, and, if you have a sense of shame, being condemned by all the hearers in place of a most severe punishment and behaving disgracefully, you will suffer pain in your own soul through conscience. For we have seen your defeat in action and have heard your promised argument. In the end, then, I do not think you will come to the inquiry as you promised; rather, to appear unashamed, you have promised as you leave to return.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you leveled preconceived judgments against me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive refers to judgments concerning the father, not necessarily the father’s own prejudices. “You cast down my preconceptions” is a grammatical alternative, but the following reminder of Simon’s failure to test the speaker favors accusations about him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in place of a most severe punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preposition can convey a replacement or an equivalent penalty. The condemnation is not made a separate physical punishment.
The wording can also mean the argument that makes your promises. The context of Simon’s promised return supports an argument he promises to present, without treating it as already delivered.
This can indicate not being ashamed or not losing face. It does not assert that Simon lacks every moral sense of shame.

source_issues.issue: The incomplete ἀλ.....νοίας, with exactly five dots, is retained literally. The main text translates the surviving giving and being-persuaded wording but does not complete this word as “signs,” “pretenses,” or any other conjecture.
The nine-dot gap and surviving νοίας are retained literally. The feminine plural “all” and possessive “your” are translated, without recovering the missing word.

The surviving partial participial stem and twelve-dot gap are retained literally after “But.” The stem relates to full assurance, but its lost completion and syntactic continuation are not restored, and no claim that Simon is now convinced is invented.

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
